title: Exam skills: listening, reading, writing, speaking and translation

tips.title: French is written longer than it sounds
tips.body: Almost every dictation error is an ending you cannot hear: the **-ent** of *ils jouent*, the silent final consonant of *petit*, an agreement like *petite*. Write what the grammar requires, not only what you heard.

tips.title: The final -e makes the consonant sound
tips.body: *Peti**t*** sounds like *peti*; *peti**te*** sounds the *t*. *Gran**d*** is nasal; *gran**de*** sounds the *d*. If you **hear** the consonant, there is probably an **-e** after it — which usually means a feminine agreement.

tips.title: Three time frames in the extended writing
tips.body: The 80–90 word task (and the Higher 130–150 word task) wants **a combination of present, past and future timeframes**, signalled clearly: *avant, maintenant, à l'avenir*. Range with accuracy beats length — a long answer in one tense scores below a shorter one in three.

tips.title: Translate, then reread in English only
tips.body: Do the translation twice: once **accounting for every French word**, then once **reading only your English** to make it natural. The first pass wins the detail marks, the second stops *I have five years* going down on the page.

tips.title: Every bullet point, every prompt
tips.body: In Writing, a bullet point not covered is content you cannot get credit for. In the role play, a prompt not answered is a mark gone. Before you finish either, count the bullets or prompts against your answer — it takes ten seconds.

why.matters: The last topic is the four papers as they will be sat, skill by skill, and it exists because each skill has a trick that is not French but exam. The dictation writes endings the ear cannot hear, so the grammar decides them. The translation must account for every word before the English is made natural. The informal writing task must show three time frames in about eighty to ninety words, and the Higher formal task in 130 to 150. The read aloud is liaisons and silent endings; the role play is every prompt, including the question. None of it is new French; all of it is marks.

examples.title: The ending you cannot hear
examples.body: *Ils jouent* and *il joue* sound the same, and the dictation plays one of them. The sound will not decide it; the sentence will: a plural subject takes *-ent*, a feminine noun takes an agreeing adjective, a participle after *être* agrees. A heard final consonant is a clue the other way, because *petite* and *grande* sound their last consonant and *petit* and *grand* do not, so a consonant you can hear usually means an *-e* you must write.

examples.title: Three time frames in eighty to ninety words
examples.body: The extended writing is short, and it has to do a great deal: every bullet, three time frames, opinions with reasons, and accurate endings. The plan that fits is one frame per bullet with a marker at the front, *avant* for the imperfect, *maintenant* for the present, *à l'avenir* for the future, and an opinion in each. Eighty to ninety words is about four sentences per frame, so there is no room for a fourth topic and no need for one.

examples.title: Translate, then read it in English only
examples.body: A translation into English has two passes. The first accounts for every word, especially the small ones that carry meaning and vanish for a careless reader: *y, en, déjà, encore, ne … que*. The second is done without looking at the French, reading the English as English until it sounds like something a person would say. *Depuis* with a present becomes *have been doing*; *venir de* becomes *have just*; an imperfect becomes *used to* or *was doing*.

steps.title: L'écoute : la compréhension et la dictée
steps.body:
**Section A — comprehension.** Questions in English, answers in English. The skill is listening for **the words that change the meaning**, not for the ones you recognise.

- **Negatives**: *ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … plus, ne … rien, ne … que*. *Je **ne** joue **plus** au foot* is *I no longer play* — the opposite of what a noun-hunter writes down.
- **Tense markers**: *hier, la semaine dernière* (past) · *d'habitude, maintenant* (present) · *demain, l'année prochaine* (future).
- **Details**: a time, a number, a price, a reason. If the question asks for two details, give two.
- **Distractors**: recordings often mention something and then reject it — *je voulais aller au cinéma, mais finalement on est restés à la maison*. The answer is the second half.

**Section B — the dictation.** You write French from French, and the marks sit in what you **cannot hear**:

- the **-ent** of a plural verb: *ils jou**ent*** sounds exactly like *il joue*
- **silent final consonants**: *peti**t***, *gran**d***, *beaucou**p***
- the **-e** that makes a consonant sound: *petite, grande, française*
- **accents**: *é* and *è* change the sound; *à* and *a* do not, but both are marked
- **liaison**: *les_amis, un_enfant, très_intéressant* — one sound, two words

Use the three hearings differently: the whole sentence, then the gaps, then a check of endings and accents.

options: joue
jouer
jouent
joues
check.solution: A plural subject takes **-ent**, which is silent: *les garçons **jouent** au foot*. It sounds identical to *joue*.

steps.title: La lecture et la traduction
steps.body:
**The Reading paper** is 60 minutes at Higher and 45 at Foundation, with questions and answers in English, and ends with a **translation into English**: a passage at Higher, five sentences at Foundation.

**Comprehension technique**: read the **question** first, then look for its answer rather than translating the whole text. Match the detail asked for — a reason, a number, an opinion — and keep the negatives.

**The translation** has to be complete and read as natural English, so do it in two passes.

**Pass one — account for every word.** The small words carry marks: *y* (there), *en* (of it / of them), *déjà* (already), *encore* (still), *ne … que* (only), *depuis* (for / since).

**Pass two — reshape the tenses.** French and English do not line up:

- *J'apprends le français **depuis** cinq ans* → *I **have been learning** French for five years* (not *I learn*)
- *Je **jouais*** → *I **used to play*** or *I **was playing***
- *Je **viens de** manger* → *I **have just** eaten*
- *Il **faisait** beau* → *the weather **was** fine*
- *On **s'est** bien **amusés*** → *we **had** a good time*

**Pass three, really**: read your English on its own, with the French covered. If it does not sound like English a person would write, fix it: aim for *natural* English once every word is accounted for.

steps.title: L'écrit : la réponse de 80 à 90 mots
steps.body: The informal writing task (Foundation Question 3, Higher Question 1) is about 80 to 90 words; the Higher formal task (Question 2) is 130 to 150 words and wants pros and cons. Both are marked on **communication and content** and on **linguistic knowledge and accuracy**. The reliable shape is one or two sentences per bullet point, with the time frames spread across them.

visuals.problem: Write about 90 words in French about your school. Mention: your subjects · your routine · what you liked at primary school · your plans for next year.

check.solution: **Avant, maintenant, à l'avenir** — past, present and future, each announced by its marker. *D'abord, ensuite, enfin* put events in order, *parce que, car, donc* give reasons, and *mais, cependant, par contre* contrast.

steps.title: L'oral : lire à haute voix, jeu de rôle, photo
steps.body:
**Read aloud.** The marks are for pronouncing French **as French**, so the rules matter more than speed.

- Leave **silent endings silent**: *ils jouent, petit, beaucoup, les enfants*.
- Make the **liaisons**: *les_amis, un_enfant, très_important, nous_avons*.
- Keep the **nasal vowels** distinct: *on, en/an, in/ain, un*.
- Never sound the **h**: *l'homme, les_heures*.
- Use the text's own **punctuation** for phrasing — a comma is a breath, a full stop a stop.
- **é** and **è** are different sounds, and *ai* is close to *è*.

**Role play.** Cover **every prompt**, one short, clear utterance each: it is marked on communication only. Ask **one** question at Foundation and **two** at Higher, so carry a bank: *À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Est-ce que vous avez… ? Où est… ?* *Vous* is natural with a stranger, but the formal register is not required.

**Picture task.** Choose one of two photos. Three moves, in order:

1. **Describe** the people, the location and the activity (the three compulsory details): *Sur la photo, il y a… · À gauche / à droite… · Ils ont l'air contents.*
2. **Opinion with a reason**: *À mon avis, c'est… parce que…*
3. **A second tense**: *Moi, l'année dernière, j'ai… · L'année prochaine, je vais…*

Then the teacher asks two questions about your own experience and opinions (at Higher the second is in a past tense), and a conversation on the same theme follows, so be ready to give opinions and justify them.

**In the read aloud questions and the picture task**, a full sentence beats a word, and a reason beats an adjective.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write *les filles jouent* and explain which letters are silent.
2. Translate into natural English: *je viens de rentrer*.
3. Name the three moves of a picture-task answer.

**Part B.**

4. Translate into natural English: *j'habite ici depuis huit ans et je n'ai jamais déménagé*.
5. Write two questions you could use for the compulsory role-play question.
6. Write one sentence in each of the three time frames about school.

**Part C.**

7. Write an 80–90 word answer on your free time, covering four bullet points and three time frames.
8. Take the answer you wrote and check: every bullet covered? three frames? every agreement right?
9. Plan the final fortnight: which skill each day, and how you would practise the dictation specifically.

For question 7, count the words — under the count loses content, well over wastes accuracy.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Write the endings you cannot hear.** In the dictation, decide the ending from the **grammar**: a plural subject takes *-ent*, a feminine noun takes an agreeing adjective, a past participle after *être* agrees. The sound will not tell you; the sentence will.

**Use the -e clue.** If you hear a final consonant, look for an *-e*: *petite, grande, française, contente*. It usually means a feminine agreement you would otherwise miss.

**Listen past the distractor.** *Je voulais…, mais finalement…* — the answer is nearly always after the *mais*.

**Translate in two passes, then read only the English.** Every word accounted for first; natural English second. *Depuis* + present becomes *have been doing*; *venir de* becomes *have just*; the imperfect becomes *used to* or *was doing*.

**Spread the tenses in the writing.** *avant · maintenant · à l'avenir* — three frames, each announced by a marker, inside 80–90 words. Range with accuracy, not length: a long answer in one tense scores below a shorter one in three.

**Vary the opinion phrases.** *À mon avis, je trouve que, selon moi, ce que j'aime, c'est…, je dirais que* — five ways of saying what *je pense que* says once.

**Cover every prompt and every bullet, then count them.** The cheapest marks in the paper, and the ones most often dropped.

**In the picture task, reach a second tense.** At Higher the teacher's second question is in a past tense anyway, and the conversation asks about past, present and future, so a description that already moves in time is practice for both.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Listening A**: English in, English out. Listen for *ne … pas / jamais / plus*, tense markers and the detail asked for; the answer often follows *mais*.
- **Dictation**: write what the **grammar** needs — the silent **-ent**, silent final consonants, agreements, accents, liaisons. Three hearings: whole, gaps, check.
- A heard final consonant usually means a following **-e** and a feminine agreement.
- **Reading**: read the question first; answer the detail, not the whole text.
- **Translation**: pass one for every word (*y, en, déjà, encore, ne … que*), pass two for natural English.
- *Depuis* + present → *have been doing*; *venir de* → *have just*; imperfect → *used to / was doing*.
- **Writing** (~80–90 words for the informal task, 130–150 for the Higher formal task): every bullet, **three time frames** — *avant, maintenant, à l'avenir* — varied opinions and connectives, accurate endings and agreements.
- **Read aloud**: silent endings silent, liaisons made, nasal vowels kept, punctuation for phrasing, *h* never sounded.
- **Role play**: every prompt, one clear utterance each, and the compulsory questions (one at Foundation, two at Higher); communication is what is marked.
- **Picture task**: describe · opinion with a reason · **a second tense**.
- Range with accuracy beats length.

questions.prompt: In **ils jouent**, which letters at the end of **jouent** are silent?
questions.solution: The **-ent** of a plural verb is silent, so *ils jouent* sounds like *il joue*.

questions.prompt: You hear *un ___ chien*, and the missing word sounds like "peti" with no final t. How is it written?
options: petite
petits
petit
petites
questions.solution: A silent final consonant means **petit**, and *un … chien* is masculine singular, so not *petits*. If you had heard the *t*, there would be an *-e* after it.

questions.prompt: Translate into natural English: **je viens de rentrer**.
questions.solution: **I have just got home.** *Venir de* + infinitive is *to have just done*. *I come from going home* translates *venir de* word for word; *I am going to get home* mistakes it for the near future; *I got home* drops *just*.
options: I have just got home
I come from going home
I am going to get home
I got home

questions.prompt: About how many words are recommended for the informal writing task (Foundation Question 3 and Higher Question 1)?
questions.solution: Around **80 to 90** words. The Higher formal task (Question 2) is 130 to 150 words, and Foundation Question 2 is 40 to 50.

questions.prompt: Translate into natural English: **je n'y vais plus**.
questions.solution: **I no longer go there.** *Ne … plus* is *no longer*, and *y* is *there*: both must appear. *I no longer go* drops *y*; *I still go there* reverses *ne … plus*; *I did not go there any more* puts the present *vais* into the past.
options: I no longer go
I no longer go there
I still go there
I did not go there any more

questions.prompt: A recording says "*Je voulais aller à la piscine, mais finalement on est allés au parc.*" Where did they go?
options: To the swimming pool
To both
Nowhere
To the park
questions.solution: The first half is what they **wanted**; *mais finalement* introduces what actually happened — **the park**.

questions.prompt: The informal writing task should be about 80 to 90 words. What is the difference between the bottom and the top of that range?
The subject is **les élèves** and the verb *travailler* sounds like "travaille". How do you write it in the present tense?
questions.solution: **Travaillent.** A plural subject takes *-ent*, which is silent, so it sounds exactly like *travaille*. Not every plural hides like this: *ils finissent* sounds its *-iss-*, unlike *il finit*.

questions.prompt: Translate into natural English: **j'habite ici depuis huit ans**.
questions.solution: **I have lived here for eight years.** *Depuis* + present becomes an English perfect. *I live here since eight years* is word for word and not English; *I lived here eight years ago* reads *depuis* as *ago*; *I lived here for eight years* suggests you have moved away.

questions.prompt: Which order builds a picture-task answer most securely?
options: Opinion, description, a second tense
A second tense, description, opinion
Description, a second tense, description again
Describe, opinion with a reason, a second tense
questions.solution: Describe what is there (the people, the location, the activity), judge it with a reason, then bring in another tense. The other orders give an opinion or a second tense before the photo has been described, or describe it twice.

questions.prompt: Translate into natural English: **quand j'étais petite, on n'avait pas d'ordinateur, mais je viens d'en acheter un**.
questions.solution: **When I was little, we didn't have a computer, but I have just bought one.** The imperfect, the negative with *d'*, *venir de* and *en* all have to appear. *I am going to buy one* reads *venir de* as a future; *we had a computer* loses the negative; *I have just bought some* misreads *en … un*, which is *one*.

questions.prompt: Why can hearing a final consonant tell you a word is feminine?
options: Feminine nouns are always longer than masculine ones
French speakers stress feminine endings more strongly
Only feminine words end in a consonant sound in French
A final consonant is usually silent, and an -e after it makes it sound
questions.solution: *Petit* ends in a silent *t*; *petit**e*** sounds it. So a consonant you can hear usually means a written **-e** — and that *-e* is most often a feminine agreement.

questions.prompt: Translate into natural English: **ça fait deux ans que je joue de la guitare, et je ne compte pas arrêter**.
questions.solution: **I have been playing the guitar for two years, and I don't intend to stop.** *Ça fait … que* + present works like *depuis*, so English needs *have been playing*; *compter* + infinitive is *to intend to*. *I played the guitar two years ago* reads it as *ago*; *I play the guitar for two years* keeps the French present; *I intend to stop* drops the negative.

The h is silent, les links to it, and the -ent is silent
Both the h and the -ent are sounded
questions.solution: The *h* of *hommes* is mute (*h muet*), so *les* links across it — *les_hommes* — and the plural **-ent** of *arrivent* stays silent. Not every *h* allows this: *les | héros* and *les | haricots* take no liaison.

examTechnique.body:
In the **dictation**, write the endings the grammar requires rather than the ones you hear: the silent **-ent**, agreements, accents, liaisons — and treat a heard final consonant as a sign of a following **-e**.

In **translation**, account for every word first, then reread only your English: *depuis* + present becomes *have been doing*, *venir de* becomes *have just*. In the **extended writing**, cover every bullet and show **three time frames** — *avant, maintenant, à l'avenir* — with range and accuracy rather than length. In **speaking**, keep silent endings silent and liaisons made, cover every role-play prompt including the question, and always reach the second tense in the picture task.
examinerErrors: Writing only what you hear in the dictation, so -ent and agreements are lost.
Missing ne … plus and giving the opposite answer.
Taking the distractor before mais as the answer.
Leaving y, en or ne … que out of a translation.
Translating depuis + present as a simple present.
Writing a long extended answer in a single tense.
Leaving a bullet point or a role-play prompt uncovered.
Ending the picture task on description and opinion with no second tense.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 candidate writes the dictation from the grammar as much as the sound — the silent *-ent*, the agreement, the accent — and treats a heard consonant as the sign of an *-e*. Translations account for every small word and are then reread as English, so *depuis* becomes *have been doing* and *venir de* becomes *have just*. The extended answer covers every bullet inside the word count and moves through three signalled time frames with varied opinion phrases and sustained accuracy. In speaking, liaisons are made and endings left silent, every prompt is covered, and the picture task always reaches its second tense.
